extracted.intended_audience: reporters and journalism students (feature and city-hall reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for finding, reporting, structuring, and writing short 'color' features and for covering city-hall beats; includes sourcing, organization, style, and professional conduct for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding color — go to places where people congregate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where does he travel when he searches for color? He goes to the places where people congregate, and where they are likely to be a little out of their routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: railroad station, trolley car or bus rides, city clerk's office (marriage licenses), hotel lobbies, buildings with elevators. Keep eyes open; half an hour of watchful waiting in such places will often yield a story. Train frequent contacts (newsstand girl, porters, clerks) to pass on little incidents they notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use everyday incidents as story seeds (watchful waiting & informants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Something will happen or something will be said before he has ridden twenty minutes that will make a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain hundreds of persons of contact and train those who frequently meet the public to pass along little incidents. Example anecdotes (redcap with seven bags; bus driver story) show ordinary moments can become color pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature definition — seminews and flexible timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'feature' story is a seminews writing, recognizable by the fact that it is as printable on Friday as on Tuesday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes news (must run at once) from feature (can run within a fortnight). Example: interview with newly elected lodge master is a feature, printable later; election story is immediate news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color story identity — writing matters more than happening
rubrics_metrics.description: As used here, a color story is a short feature... a brief episodic bit, in which 'the way it's written' rather than the happening itself provides the gleam and sparkle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes craft and presentation: the reporter's manner of writing is the primary source of interest for color pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long feature essentials — gather and organize information
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing the long feature is largely a matter of: (i) gathering information; (2) organizing this information so that it is easy to follow and a pleasure to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long features often grow from a news event and should spend most space explaining background, how systems work, why repairs needed, who will make them, etc. Good reporting (information gathering) is as necessary for a feature as for straight news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-in with a news peg to make the feature timely
rubrics_metrics.description: An imperative in the feature story is a tie-in with the news peg which makes the feature timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tie-in may be a few words or a paragraph but must explain why the topic is of present interest (example: No. 42 train being discontinued 'Sunday after sixty years of operation'). Without the peg, a long amplification is useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature style and lead variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of the feature is essentially that of the news story, with emphasis at the top rather than at the bottom of the paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A news story likely has a one-paragraph lead; a feature may have a several-paragraph introduction, begin with stage-setting, history, or mood writing, and still must come quickly to the news peg. If a news lead is used, it may be followed by a five-W statement; features need not follow standard news story form unless desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature as amplification — avoid stylistic tricks without reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature is an 'amplification' of the news. Young reporters sometimes attempt this amplifying on the basis of tricks with words. A feature forged in this manner isn't of honest metal; it is soft at the core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reporting (thorough factual material and interviews) is essential; viewing features as an escape from reporting leads to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: organize information in coherent blocks and use refrains
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure is dependent entirely upon the demands of coherence. Information is arranged in blocks, so that an aspect of a topic is treated completely in one section of the story instead of being diffused in several sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An important exception: a mood-provoking or 'theme song' bit may be used recurrently to keep the feature at the same pitch or intensity. Where news tapers at the end, a feature may close with a snapper as powerful as the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources & idea-generation for features
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding subjects for features demands nothing more than alertness. Almost every issue of the newspaper contains suggestions for several feature stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straight-news accounts (Daily Fire Record), building permits, calendar events, notices of local changes, out-of-town papers, and statistics. Examples: fire chief interviews, rabies restraint news peg, history from historical society, annual stories timed to calendar events, consumer/policy features tied to distant tragedies or local preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a 'future book' or ledger of story ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly as the city editor has a future book, so should the feature-story specialist have a ledger in which to record suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record topics that aren't ripe now but will be timely later (example: iceboat story noted in summer to use in winter). Prevents forgetting worthwhile ideas and ensures timely follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fiction devices, mood writing, and selected quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the short color story, the devices of fiction are desirable also in the feature... mood-provoking bits and carefully chosen quotes augment the keynote of sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the analyzed feature: unusual beginnings, careful background placement, understatement for effect, repetition for emphasis, 'change of pace' to relieve tension. Choose quotes that support and augment the story's key themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness in expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Freshness in expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cited as a quality illustrated by the example feature (means original, vivid phrasing that keeps the story lively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful structure with no overlapping facets
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful structure, with no overlapping of facets or aspects except the 'theme song' refrain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit quality: arrange aspects into distinct blocks so each is treated completely in one section; avoid diffusing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of factual material / thorough reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: An abundance of factual material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example emphasizes thorough interviewing and inclusion of specific facts (dates, ages, unit designations, quotes). Feature writing depends on detailed, specific reporting to be credible and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the city-hall 'language' — beat expertise and translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning a new language. Reporter must learn the speech of city-hall folk so he can find out their problems, ways of thinking, and prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study persistently; don't 'pick up' familiarity. Translate official jargon into vocabulary of the ordinary reader (example: explain 'committee of the whole' as 'thereby excluding the public from the discussion'). Beat expertise marks the capable city-hall reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to 'look blank' and exercise judgment/diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing when to look blank and say nothing. Municipal employees put every word on the scales before they say it; a carelessly phrased remark may stir a controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish background information from material made for publication. Be a diplomat and confidant of officials without being partisan. Avoid printing rumors and gossip; cultivate officials' trust so they will speak on record. Phrase remarks to present intent rather than crudity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with lucidity and sparkle — make complex/boring subjects interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing like a Pulitzer prize winner. If his stories are opaque, his readers will be few. Governmental news is congenitally complex; unless it is presented attractively, sparklingly, readers slight it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lucidity isn't enough — make statistics and technical municipal reports (sealer of weights and measures, etc.) interesting. Use attractive presentation and good writing craft to hold readers' attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat longevity and becoming an authority
rubrics_metrics.description: City-hall men often are greenhorns until they have been on the beat a year; when combined with expertness and true writing skill he is one of reporting's aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that training a successor is time-consuming; being an authority gives psychological satisfaction and city influence. Persistent study and experience are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand municipal organization and roles to report accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: City-hall organization is unstandardized, but in broad outlines municipal organization lends itself to classification (executive/policy-making, legislative, liaison, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know functions and nuances of mayor, city manager, city council, city clerk, and committees to interpret actions and predict outcomes (e.g., how mayor's veto power, charter specs, or committee procedure affect policy). Understanding these structures helps translate technicalities for readers and to find newsworthy angles (state interference with city home-rule example).
